Abstract:

While the discourse of the Anthropocene has established the human species as a geological force causing significant ecological disruption, it obscures the fact that the impacts of environmental degradation and Climate Change are differentially experienced by different people. The Environmental Justice Movement, along with other grassroots movements in the Global South, have historically been emphasising how the socially marginalised disproportionately bear the burden of a degrading environment. For postcolonial countries like India, the peripheral position in the capitalist neocolonial world system intensifies environmental injustices produced by the country&amprsquos entrenched structural inequalities of class, caste, ethnicity, and gender, among others. On this premise, this study undertakes a postcolonial ecocritical analysis of select Indian English narratives namely, Pankaj Sekhsaria&amprsquos The Last Wave (2014), Kiran Nagarkar&amprsquos Jasoda (2017), Kavery Nambisan&amprsquos The Story that Must Not Be Told (2010), and Nitin Sekar&amprsquos What&amprsquos Left of the Jungle: A Conservation Story (2022), to interrogate how contemporary literature represents and reimagines the interconnections between environmental issues and social justice. Through this analysis, this study explores tribal land, gendered body, urban space, and multispecies relations as sites where environmental injustices manifest in India. It questions how access to environmental benefits and protection from environmental harm are shaped by broader structural relations of power, which often silence marginalised voices and obscure their lived experiences. Thus, this study upholds the redefinition of the &amplsquoenvironment&amprsquo as more than a nostalgic pristine wilderness, foregrounding it instead as a political and historical site of power struggle. The convergence of Environmental Justice, postcolonial studies, and literary studies underscores that the environmental crisis is also a cultural phenomenon, reproduced and shaped by history and discourse. It also emphasises the role of literature in archiving subaltern narratives as well as contributing to environmental activism. &nbsp

Keywords: Environmental Justice, Postcolonialism, Ecocriticism, Indian English Literature, Social Inequalities&nbsp
